seatMission: Align roles, skills, incentives and adoption.
seatResponsibilities: Design organization, roles, skills, incentives, change and adoption.

criterionDimensions.name: Ethics, fairness, and durable adoption governance

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I design organizational structures from required outcomes and capabilities rather than copying fashionable org charts.
I distinguish structural problems from process, leadership, skill, incentive, tooling, and capacity problems before recommending reorganization.
I make explicit how each organizational unit contributes to customer, operational, financial, risk, or strategic outcomes.
I test whether spans, layers, reporting lines, and coordination mechanisms match the complexity and decision load of the work.
I identify duplicated, fragmented, or orphaned responsibilities that create delay, conflict, or accountability gaps.
I design interfaces between functions so cross-functional work has clear handoffs, shared outcomes, and escalation paths.
I preserve necessary separation of duties where combining roles would weaken control, independence, or assurance.
I distinguish permanent organization design from temporary program, project, or incident structures.
I evaluate organization changes against expected benefits, transition cost, disruption risk, and reversibility.
I avoid using reorganization as a substitute for resolving unclear strategy, priorities, or decision rights.
I define roles in terms of accountable outcomes, decisions, and services rather than lists of activities alone.
I assign one clearly accountable owner for each material result while distinguishing contributors, approvers, advisors, and informed parties.
I detect accountability that is nominal because the assigned owner lacks authority, information, budget, capacity, or control.
I distinguish responsibility for doing work from accountability for the result the work must produce.
I make decision rights explicit enough that routine choices do not require unnecessary executive escalation.
I identify decisions that require consultation or independent approval because of risk, law, control, or stakeholder impact.
I prevent RACI-style artifacts from hiding unresolved conflict by testing whether real participants agree on ownership.
I design escalation paths with thresholds, recipients, evidence requirements, and expected response times.
I review role boundaries when work repeatedly falls between teams, is duplicated, or depends on informal heroics.
I update role and decision-right definitions when operating reality proves the documented model inaccurate.
I distinguish missing skill from insufficient capacity, weak process, poor tooling, unclear direction, or low motivation.
I identify the critical capabilities required by the operating model and map them to roles, teams, partners, or automation.
I assess capability using observable performance evidence rather than credentials or self-reported confidence alone.
I quantify workload and available capacity sufficiently to detect chronic overload, idle specialization, and hidden queues.
I recognize when a role requires depth that cannot be economically maintained internally and evaluate external or shared capability options.
I build learning priorities from real performance gaps and future capability needs rather than generic training catalogs.
I protect scarce expert capacity from low-value work through role design, delegation, automation, and better demand management.
I identify single points of human capability failure and establish succession, redundancy, documentation, or cross-training where justified.
I account for learning curves and temporary productivity loss when introducing new roles, systems, or processes.
I verify that staffing recommendations remain economically sustainable at expected demand levels.
I test whether incentives reward the behaviors and outcomes the operating model actually needs.
I identify incentive conflicts that cause local optimization at the expense of enterprise, customer, quality, or risk outcomes.
I avoid performance measures that reward volume while ignoring value, quality, rework, harm, or downstream cost.
I distinguish intrinsic professional standards, social norms, and formal incentives when diagnosing behavior.
I design performance expectations that employees can materially influence through their work.
I recognize when targets become dysfunctional because people must game definitions, delay bad news, or sacrifice long-term value to achieve them.
I align recognition and consequences with accountable outcomes while preserving proportionality and due process.
I test compensation or bonus mechanics for unintended effects across teams, customer segments, and time horizons.
I separate performance-management problems from structural barriers that make the expected result unattainable.
I revise incentives when evidence shows they drive materially different behavior from what was intended.
I identify who gains, loses, changes identity, loses autonomy, gains burden, or faces uncertainty because of an organizational change.
I assess readiness separately for leadership commitment, manager capability, employee understanding, process maturity, technology readiness, and local capacity.
I distinguish stated support from demonstrated willingness to change decisions, routines, resources, and measures.
I identify informal leaders, trusted experts, and social networks that materially influence adoption beyond the formal org chart.
I surface legitimate objections and operational constraints rather than labeling all resistance as attitude problems.
I sequence change so prerequisite capabilities, policies, tooling, and manager behaviors exist before demanding new frontline behavior.
I design transition support proportionate to change magnitude, reversibility, risk, and population affected.
I account for change saturation when multiple initiatives compete for the same attention, managers, experts, or frontline capacity.
I establish explicit stop, adapt, or defer conditions when adoption risk becomes greater than expected value.
I preserve evidence of stakeholder concerns and responses so unresolved risks are visible rather than edited out of the change narrative.
I define adoption as observable use and behavior in real work rather than attendance, communication reach, or system login alone.
I specify the critical behaviors that must start, stop, continue, or improve for the change to create value.
I measure whether new behavior persists after launch support and executive attention decline.
I identify friction, cognitive load, policy conflict, tool limitations, and local workarounds that prevent desired behavior.
I distinguish inability, uncertainty, disagreement, overload, and unwillingness when adoption falls short.
I design prompts, defaults, feedback, coaching, and workflow changes that make the desired behavior easier to perform correctly.
I test adoption across roles, locations, shifts, tenure levels, and edge conditions rather than relying on aggregate averages.
I use qualitative field evidence alongside usage metrics to explain why adoption is or is not occurring.
I remove obsolete procedures, metrics, permissions, and tools that continue to reinforce the old behavior.
I connect adoption evidence to business, customer, quality, risk, or operational outcomes rather than treating adoption as an end in itself.
I define the leadership behaviors required to sustain the target operating model and test whether leaders actually demonstrate them.
I distinguish leadership sponsorship from operational ownership and ensure both exist where needed.
I identify when leaders create ambiguity by sending conflicting priorities, tolerating exceptions, or rewarding behavior contrary to the stated change.
I design manager routines for coaching, prioritization, issue escalation, workload balancing, and performance feedback.
I ensure managers receive the information and authority needed to resolve routine problems close to the work.
I detect management systems that depend on recurring heroics, private spreadsheets, informal favors, or executive intervention.
I make leadership commitments observable through resource choices, meeting behavior, decisions, and consequences.
I protect psychological safety for reporting errors, risks, dissent, and bad news without weakening accountability for avoidable misconduct.
I recognize when leadership turnover or role vacancies materially threaten adoption and include mitigation in the plan.
I evaluate whether management cadence produces decisions and learning rather than meetings, status theater, and reporting burden.
I connect workforce planning to demand, capability, productivity, automation, attrition, succession, and strategic scenarios.
I distinguish roles that should be hired, developed, redeployed, contracted, automated, consolidated, or retired.
I identify hiring criteria from actual job outcomes and evidence requirements rather than inflated lists of technologies or credentials.
I assess onboarding by time to safe, independent, value-producing performance rather than completion of orientation activities.
I design career and development paths that retain critical capability without requiring artificial management promotions.
I include succession and continuity planning for roles whose absence would materially disrupt operations or decisions.
I evaluate retention risk using role scarcity, workload, manager quality, compensation, growth, purpose, and labor-market evidence.
I treat layoffs, role elimination, and redeployment as operating-model decisions with human, legal, knowledge, and execution consequences.
I preserve critical institutional knowledge during transitions through deliberate transfer, documentation, shadowing, and overlap where justified.
I monitor whether workforce decisions improve sustainable capability rather than producing short-term cost reduction followed by hidden rework or rehiring.
I define a small set of measures that distinguish organizational capacity, behavior, adoption, performance, and outcomes.
I establish baselines before claiming that an organization or people intervention caused improvement.
I separate leading indicators of behavior change from lagging business outcomes and avoid treating either as sufficient alone.
I segment organizational metrics so aggregate averages do not hide failing teams, locations, roles, or demographic groups.
I combine quantitative measures with interviews, observation, case evidence, and operational data when interpreting organizational health.
I distinguish correlation between an intervention and an outcome from credible evidence that the intervention caused the outcome.
I track unintended consequences such as burnout, turnover, workarounds, quality loss, silence, or control weakness.
I define evidence thresholds for scaling, adapting, or stopping organization and adoption interventions.
I protect confidentiality and appropriate access when using employee, performance, or sensitive workforce evidence.
I report uncertainty and contradictory organizational evidence instead of forcing a single optimistic narrative.
I evaluate organization and people decisions for fairness, proportionality, dignity, legal obligations, and foreseeable human impact.
I avoid using analytics, automation, or AI for workforce decisions without appropriate validity, oversight, explainability, and appeal mechanisms.
I distinguish equal treatment from equitable treatment when roles, constraints, risk, and reasonable accommodations differ.
I design governance so affected people can surface errors, unintended consequences, and legitimate exceptions.
I prevent confidential employee information from being exposed merely because it is useful for management analysis.
I ensure adoption pressure does not coerce unsafe, unlawful, deceptive, or professionally improper behavior.
I preserve documented rationale for material organization, talent, and adoption decisions that affect people.
I define who may approve exceptions and how exception patterns trigger review of the underlying policy or design.
I evaluate whether organizational improvements remain sustainable after consultants, project teams, and launch incentives leave.
I treat durable adoption as achieved only when the target behavior, supporting system, accountability, and evidence all persist in normal operations.
